{{Short description|Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan}} {{About|a Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan|other topics translated as "Temple of the Golden Pavilion" or "Golden Pavilion Temple" in English|Temple of the Golden Pavilion (disambiguation)}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Rokuon-ji | native_name = {{lang|ja|鹿苑寺}} | image = Kinkaku-ji the Golden Temple in Kyoto overlooking the lake - high rez.JPG | image_size = 350 | alt = | caption = The ''shariden'' at Rokuon-ji,
commonly known as the Golden Pavilion (''Kinkakuji'') {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=220}} | map_type = Japan | map_size = | map_alt = | map_caption = | location = 1 Kinkakuji-chō, [[:en:Kita-ku, Kyoto|Kita-ku]], [[:en:Kyoto|Kyōto]], [[:en:Kyoto Prefecture|Kyoto Prefecture]]{{cite web |url=http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/arrange/attractions/facilities/gardens/83dn3a000000ee6g.html |title=Tourist Facilities of Japan - Kinkaku-ji Temple Garden |publisher=Japan National Tourism Organization |access-date=2010-07-15}} | coordinates = {{Coord|35.0395|N|135.7285|E|format=dms|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | religious_affiliation = [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] | sect =[[Zen]], [[Rinzai]] sect, [[Shōkoku-ji]] school | deity = [[:en:Avalokiteśvara|Kannon Bosatsu]] (Avalokiteśvara) | country = Japan | functional_status = | website = {{URL|https://www.shokoku-ji.jp/en/kinkakuji/|www.shokoku-ji.jp/en/kinkakuji/}} | founded_by = [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshimitsu|Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]] | year_completed = 1397
1955 (reconstruction) }} {{nihongo|'''Kinkaku-ji'''|金閣寺||{{literally}} 'Temple of the Golden Pavilion'}}, officially named {{nihongo|'''Rokuon-ji'''|鹿苑寺||{{literally|[[Sarnath|Deer Garden]] Temple}}}}, is a [[Zen]] [[:en:Buddhist temples in Japan|Buddhist temple]] in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{cite web |url=http://www.orientalarchitecture.com/japan/kyoto/kinkakuji.php |title=Kinkakuji Temple - 金阁寺, Kyoto, Japan |publisher=Oriental Architecture |access-date=2010-07-13}} It is one of the most popular buildings in Kyoto, attracting many visitors annually.Bornoff, Nicholas (2000). ''The National Geographic Traveler: Japan''. National Geographic Society. {{ISBN|0-7922-7563-2}}. It is designated as a National Special Historic Site, a National Special Landscape and is one of 17 locations making up the [[:en:Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)|Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto]] which are [[World Heritage Site]]s.{{cite web |url=http://kyoto.asanoxn.com/places/ps_popularity.htm |title=Places of Interest in Kyoto (Top 15 most visited places in Kyoto by visitors from overseas) |publisher=Asano Noboru |access-date=2010-07-15}} ==History== is peeling off due to deterioration over time.]] The site of Kinkaku-ji was originally a villa called ''Kitayama-dai'' (北山第), belonging to a powerful statesman, [[Saionji Kintsune]].{{cite web |url=http://kyoto.asanoxn.com/places/kinkaku/kinkakuji.htm |title=Kinkaku-ji in Kyoto |publisher=Asano Noboru |access-date=2010-07-15}} Kinkaku-ji's history dates to 1397, when the villa was purchased from the Saionji family by ''[[shōgun]]'' [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshimitsu|Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]] and transformed into the Kinkaku-ji complex. When Yoshimitsu died the building was converted into a [[Zen Buddhism|Zen]] temple by his son, according to his wishes.Scott, David (1996). ''Exploring Japan''. Fodor's Travel Publications, Inc. {{ISBN|0-679-03011-5}}.{{page number|date=June 2020}} During the [[:en:Ōnin war|Ōnin war]] (1467–1477), all of the buildings in the complex aside from the pavilion were burned down. On 2 July 1950, at 2:30 am, the pavilion was burned down{{cite web |last1=Cartwright |first1=Mark |title=Kinkakuji |url=https://www.worldhistory.org/Kinkakuji/ |website=World History Encyclopedia |publisher=UNESCO |access-date=23 March 2021}} by a 22-year-old novice monk, Hayashi Yoken ([[:en:Kinkaku-ji arson|Kinkaku-ji arson incident]]), who then attempted suicide on the Daimon-ji hill behind the building. He survived, and was subsequently taken into custody. The monk was sentenced to seven years in prison, but was released because of mental illnesses ([[persecution complex]] and [[schizophrenia]]) on 29 September 1955; he died of [[tuberculosis]] in March 1956.{{cite book|author=Albert Borowitz|title=Terrorism for self-glorification: the Herostratos syndrome|url=https://archive.org/details/terrorismforself0000boro|url-access=registration|access-date=1 July 2011|year=2005|publisher=Kent State University Press|isbn=978-0-87338-818-4|pages=[https://archive.org/details/terrorismforself0000boro/page/49 49]–62}} See: [[:en:Herostratos syndrome|Herostratos syndrome]] During the fire, the original statue of Ashikaga Yoshimitsu was lost to the flames (now restored). A fictionalized version of these events is at the center of [[Yukio Mishima]]'s 1956 book ''[[The Temple of the Golden Pavilion]]'', and another in the ballet ''[[RAkU (ballet)| RAkU]]''. The present pavilion structure dates from 1955, when it was rebuilt. The pavilion is three stories high, {{convert|12.5|m|ft|adj=off|sp=us|abbr=off|-1}} in height.Young, David, and Michiko Young. The art of Japanese Architecture. North Claredon, VT: Turtle Publishing, 2007. N. pag. Print.{{page number|date=June 2020}} The reconstruction is said to be a close copy of the original, although some have questioned whether such an extensive gold-leaf coating was used on the original structure. In 1984, it was discovered that the gold leaf on the reconstructed building had peeled off, and from 1986 to 1987, it was replaced with 0.5 μm gold leaf, five times the thickness of the gold leaf on the reconstructed building. Although Japanese gold leaf has become thinner with the passage of time due to improved technology, the 0.5 μm gold leaf is as thick as traditional Japanese gold leaf.{{cite web|url=http://www.koetsuan.jp/kinkaku/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211023011422/http://www.koetsuan.jp/kinkaku/index.html|script-title=ja:金閣寺大修復 金閣修復 五倍箔|language=ja|author=Kazuo Yaguchi|archive-date=23 October 2021|access-date=30 October 2022}} Additionally, the interior of the building, including the paintings and Yoshimitsu's statue, were also restored. Finally, the roof was restored in 2003. The name Kinkaku (金閣 ''gold pavilion'') is derived from the gold leaf that the pavilion is covered in. Gold was an important addition to the pavilion because of its underlying meaning. The gold employed was intended to mitigate and purify any pollution or negative thoughts and feelings towards death.Gerhart, Karen M. The material culture of Death in medieval Japan. N.p.: University of Hawaii Press, 2009. N. pag. Print.{{page number|date=June 2020}} Other than the symbolic meaning behind the gold leaf, the Muromachi period heavily relied on visual excesses. With the focus on the Golden Pavilion, the way that the structure is mainly covered in that material creates an impression that stands out because of the sunlight reflecting and the effect the reflection creates on the pond. {{clear|left}} ==Design details== [[File:Kinkaku-ji 04.jpg|thumb|right|Roof ornament]] The {{nihongo|Golden Pavilion|金閣|Kinkaku}} is a three-story building on the grounds of the Rokuon-ji temple complex. The top two stories of the pavilion are covered with pure [[:en:Gold leaf|Gold leaf]]. The pavilion functions as a ''shariden'' (舎利殿), housing relics of the [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Buddha]] (Buddha's Ashes). The building was an important model for [[Ginkaku-ji]] (Silver Pavilion Temple) and [[Shōkoku-ji]], which are also located in Kyoto. When these buildings were constructed, [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshimasa|Ashikaga Yoshimasa]] employed the styles used at Kinkaku-ji and even borrowed the names of its second and third floors. ===Architectural design=== [[File:Kinkakuji Kyoto05s3s3990.jpg|thumb|left|The fishing deck and small islets at the rear of the pavilion]] The pavilion successfully incorporates three distinct styles of architecture, which are shinden, samurai and zen, specifically on each floor. Each floor of the Kinkaku uses a different architectural style. The first floor, called ''The Chamber of Dharma Waters'' (法水院, Hō-sui-in), is rendered in ''[[shinden-zukuri]]'' style, reminiscent of the residential style of the 11th century [[:en:Heian period|Heian]] imperial aristocracy. It is evocative of the Shinden palace style. It is designed as an open space with adjacent verandas and uses natural, unpainted wood and white plaster. This helps to emphasize the surrounding landscape. The walls and fenestration also affect the views from inside the pavilion. Most of the walls are made of shutters that can vary the amount of light and air into the pavilion and change the view by controlling the shutters' heights. The second floor, called ''The Tower of Sound Waves'' (潮音洞, Chō-on-dō ), is built in the style of warrior aristocrats, or ''[[:en:Shinden-zukuri|Shinden-zukuri]]''. On this floor, sliding wood doors and latticed windows create a feeling of impermanence. The second floor also contains a Buddha Hall and a shrine dedicated to the goddess of mercy, Kannon. The third floor is built in traditional [[:en:Chinese Chán|Chinese ''chán'']] (Jpn. [[zen]]) style, also known as ''zenshū-[[:en:Main Hall (Japanese Buddhism)|Main Hall (Japanese Buddhism)]]-zukuri''. It is called the ''Cupola of the Ultimate'' (究竟頂, Kukkyō-chō). The zen typology depicts a more religious ambiance in the pavilion, as was popular during the Muromachi period. The roof is in a thatched pyramid with shingles.Young, David, Michiko Young, and Tan Hong. The material culture of Death in medieval Japan. North Claredon, VT: Turtle Publishing, 2005. N. pag. Print. The building is topped with a bronze [[:en:Fenghuang|''hōō'']] (phoenix) ornament. From the outside, viewers can see gold plating added to the upper stories of the pavilion. The gold leaf covering the upper stories hints at what is housed inside: the shrines. The outside is a reflection of the inside. The elements of nature, death, religion, are formed together to create this connection between the pavilion and outside intrusions. ===Garden design=== The Golden Pavilion is set in a Japanese {{nihongo|strolling garden|回遊式庭園|kaiyū-shiki-teien|lit. a landscape garden in the go-round style}}. The location implements the idea of [[:en:Borrowing of scenery ("shakkei")|Borrowing of scenery ("shakkei")]] that integrates the outside and the inside, creating an extension of the views surrounding the pavilion and connecting it with the outside world. The pavilion extends over a pond, called {{nihongo|''Kyōko-chi''|鏡湖池|Mirror Pond}}, that reflects the building. The pond contains 10 smaller islands. The zen typology is seen through the rock composition; the bridges and plants are arranged in a specific way to represent famous places in Chinese and Japanese literature. Vantage points and focal points were established because of the strategic placement of the pavilion to view the gardens surrounding the pavilion. A small {{nihongo|fishing hall|釣殿|tsuri-dono}} or roofed deck is attached to the rear of the pavilion building, allowing a small boat to be moored under it. The pavilion grounds were built according to descriptions of the [[Pure Land Buddhism#Early history|Western Paradise of the Buddha Amida]], intending to illustrate a harmony between heaven and earth. The largest [[:en:Islet|Islet]] in the pond represents the Japanese islands. The four stones forming a straight line in the pond near the pavilion are intended to represent sailboats anchored at night, bound for the ''Isle of Eternal Life'' in Chinese mythology. The garden complex is an excellent example of [[Muromachi period]] garden design.''Eyewitness Travel Guides: Japan''. Dorling Kindersley Publishing (2000). {{ISBN|0-7894-5545-5}}. The Muromachi period is considered to be a classical age of Japanese garden design.“Pregil, Philip, and Nancy Volkman. Landscapes in History: Design and Planning in the Eastern and Western tradition. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons Inc., 1992. N. pag. Print.”. The correlation between buildings and its settings were greatly emphasized during this period. It was an artistic way to integrate the structure within the landscape. The garden designs were characterized by a reduction in scale, a more central purpose, and a distinct setting.Boults, Elizabeth, and Chip Sullivan. Illustrated History of Landscape Design. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons INc., 2010. N. pag. Print. A minimalistic approach was brought to the garden design by recreating larger landscapes in a smaller scale around a structure. ==Gallery== File:1930s Japan Travel Poster - 15.jpg|1930s travel poster File:Kinkaku-ji entrance.jpg|Entrance and ticket booth File:Kinkaku-ji close up.jpg|Kinkaku-ji close up File:Kinkaku-ji 03.jpg|Interior File:Kinkaku-ji garden.jpg|Kinkaku-ji garden File:Golden Pavillion 2010 03 29 32.jpg|The lower pond File:Yōshū Chikanobu Kinkaku haiken.jpg|[[Toyohara Chikanobu]] File:Kyoto-Kinkaku-ji-White-Snake.jpg|White Snake Pagoda of Kinkaku-ji File:Kinkaku-ji temple in Kyoto.jpg|Kinkaku-Ji, Kyoto in May 2019 File:Kinkakuji Keychain from Japan, from personal collection, photographed by Yogabrata Chakraborty, on May 6, 2023.jpg|Kinkaku-ji keychain ==See also== {{Portal|Japan|Religion|Gardening|Architecture}} * [[The Temple of the Golden Pavilion]] by Yukio Mishima, a novel loosely based on the 1950 destruction of Kinkaku-ji * [[:en:Buntenkaku|Buntenkaku]] in Nagoya, modeled after the Golden Pavilion * [[Ginkaku-ji]] * [[Shōkoku-ji]] * [[:en:Chūson-ji|Chūson-ji]] with golden Konjiki-dō * [[:en:Golden Tea Room|Golden Tea Room]] * [[:en:List of Special Places of Scenic Beauty, Special Historic Sites and Special Natural Monuments|List of Special Places of Scenic Beauty, Special Historic Sites and Special Natural Monuments]] * [[:en:Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)|Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)]] ==Notes== {{reflist|30em}} == References == * Boults, Elizabeth, and Chip Sullivan. ''Illustrated History of Landscape Design''. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2010. * Gerhart, Karen M. ''The Material Culture of Death in Medieval Japan''. Honolulu: University of Hawaii Press, 2009. * Pregil, Philip, and Nancy Volkman. ''Landscapes in History: Design and Planning in the Eastern and Western Tradition''. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 1992. * Young, David, and Michiko Young. ''The Art of Japanese Architecture''. North Claredon, VT: Tuttle Publishing, 2007. * Young, David, Michiko Young, and Tan Hong. ''Introduction to Japanese Architecture''. North Claredon, VT: Periplus, 2005. == Further reading == *{{cite book |last= Kawaguchi |first= Yoko |title= Japanese Zen Gardens |location= London |publisher= Francis Lincoln |date= 2014 |type= Hardback |isbn= 978-0-7112-3447-5}} *[[Schirokauer, Conrad]]; Lurie, David; Gay, Suzanne (2005). A Brief History of Japanese Civilization. Wadsworth Publishing. {{ISBN|978-0-618-91522-4}}. OCLC 144227752. ==External links== {{Commons Category:11]] [[Category|Kinkaku-ji}} * [https://www.shokoku-ji.jp/en/kinkakuji/ Official site of Kinkaku-ji] * [http://www.orientalarchitecture.com/japan/kyoto/kinkakuji.php Oriental Architecture – Kinkakuji Temple] * [https://www.omamori.com/en/4_kinkaku-ji Omamori Charms Amulets of Kinkaku-ji Temple] * {{Osmway|98115917}} {{World Heritage Kyoto}} {{Buddhist temples in Japan}} {{draft categories| [[Category:1397 establishments]] [[Category:14th-century Buddhist temples]] [[Category:20th-century Buddhist temples]] [[Category:Buddhist temples in Kyoto]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Japan]] [[Category:Myoshin-ji temples]] [[Category:Rebuilt buildings and structures in Japan]] [[Category:Religious buildings and structures completed in 1955]] [[Category:Special Historic Sites]] [[Category:Special Places of Scenic Beauty]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]] }} [[image:Japon-1886-41.jpg|thumb|left|Painted photograph of the Golden Pavilion in 1885. The [[:en:Gold leaf|Gold leaf]] [[image:Burned Kinkaku.jpg|thumb|left|Golden Pavilion following the 1950 arson]] [[sn:Kinkaku-ji]] [[en:Kinkaku-ji]] [[Category:Pages without translation templates]] [[ar:كينكاكو-جي]] [[arz:كينكاكو جى]] [[az:Kinkaku məbədi]] [[bg:Кинкаку-джи]] [[bn:কিঙ্কাকু-জি]] [[br:Kinkaku-ji]] [[bxr:Кинкаку-дзи]] [[ca:Kinkaku-ji]] [[cs:Kinkakudži]] [[da:Kinkaku-ji]] [[de:Kinkaku-ji]] [[eo:Rokuonji]] [[es:Kinkaku-ji]] [[eu:Kinkaku-ji]] [[fa:کینکاکو-جی]] [[fi:Kinkaku-ji]] [[fr:Kinkaku-ji]] [[he:המקדש המוזהב]] [[hi:किंकाकू जी]] [[hr:Kinkaku]] [[hu:Kinkakudzsi]] [[hy:Կինկակու]] [[id:Kinkaku-ji]] [[it:Kinkaku-ji]] [[ja:鹿苑寺]] [[ka:კინკაკუ-ძი]] [[kk:Кинкаку-дзи]] [[ko:로쿠온지]] [[la:Kinkaku-ji]] [[lt:Kinkakudži]] [[mk:Кинкаку-џи]] [[ms:Kinkaku-ji]] [[my:ရွှေကျောင်းတော်]] [[nl:Kinkaku-ji]] [[nn:Kinkaku-ji]] [[pl:Złoty Pawilon]] [[pt:Kinkaku-ji]] [[ru:Кинкаку-дзи]] [[sh:Kinkaku]] [[si:ස්වර්ණමණ්ඩපාරාමය]] [[simple:Kinkaku-ji]] [[sk:Kinkakudži]] [[sl:Kinkaku-dži]] [[sr:Кинкаку-ђи]] [[sv:Kinkaku-ji]] [[ta:கிங்காகு ஜி]] [[th:คิงกากูจิ]] [[tr:Kinkaku-ji]] [[tt:Кинкаку-җи]] [[uk:Монастир Кінкаку]] [[vi:Kinkakuji]] [[war:Kinkaku-ji]] [[zh:鹿苑寺]] [[zh-yue:金閣寺]] [[Category:pages with valid en interwikis 2]]

The art of Japanese Architecture. North Claredon, VT: Turtle Publishing, 2007. N. pag. Print.{{page number|date=June 2020}} The reconstruction is said to be a close copy of the original, although some have questioned whether such an extensive gold-leaf coating was used on the original structure. In 1984, it was discovered that the gold leaf on the reconstructed building had peeled off, and from 1986 to 1987, it was replaced with 0.5 μm gold leaf, five times the thickness of the gold leaf on the reconstructed building. Although Japanese gold leaf has become thinner with the passage of time due to improved technology, the 0.5 μm gold leaf is as thick as traditional Japanese gold leaf.{{cite web|url=http://www.koetsuan.jp/kinkaku/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211023011422/http://www.koetsuan.jp/kinkaku/index.html|script-title=ja:金閣寺大修復 金閣修復 五倍箔|language=ja|author=Kazuo Yaguchi|archive-date=23 October 2021|access-date=30 October 2022}} Additionally, the interior of the building, including the paintings and Yoshimitsu's statue, were also restored. Finally, the roof was restored in 2003. The name Kinkaku (金閣 ''gold pavilion'') is derived from the gold leaf that the pavilion is covered in. Gold was an important addition to the pavilion because of its underlying meaning. The gold employed was intended to mitigate and purify any pollution or negative thoughts and feelings towards death.Gerhart, Karen M. The material culture of Death in medieval Japan. N.p.: University of Hawaii Press, 2009. N. pag. Print.{{page number|date=June 2020}} Other than the symbolic meaning behind the gold leaf, the Muromachi period heavily relied on visual excesses. With the focus on the Golden Pavilion, the way that the structure is mainly covered in that material creates an impression that stands out because of the sunlight reflecting and the effect the reflection creates on the pond. {{clear|left}} ==Design details== [[File:Kinkaku-ji 04.jpg|thumb|right|Roof ornament]] The {{nihongo|Golden Pavilion|金閣|Kinkaku}} is a three-story building on the grounds of the Rokuon-ji temple complex. The top two stories of the pavilion are covered with pure [[:en:Gold leaf|Gold leaf]]. The pavilion functions as a ''shariden'' (舎利殿), housing relics of the [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Buddha]] (Buddha's Ashes). The building was an important model for [[Ginkaku-ji]] (Silver Pavilion Temple) and [[Shōkoku-ji]], which are also located in Kyoto. When these buildings were constructed, [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshimasa|Ashikaga Yoshimasa]] employed the styles used at Kinkaku-ji and even borrowed the names of its second and third floors. ===Architectural design=== [[File:Kinkakuji Kyoto05s3s3990.jpg|thumb|left|The fishing deck and small islets at the rear of the pavilion]] The pavilion successfully incorporates three distinct styles of architecture, which are shinden, samurai and zen, specifically on each floor. Each floor of the Kinkaku uses a different architectural style. The first floor, called ''The Chamber of Dharma Waters'' (法水院, Hō-sui-in), is rendered in ''[[shinden-zukuri]]'' style, reminiscent of the residential style of the 11th century [[:en:Heian period|Heian]] imperial aristocracy. It is evocative of the Shinden palace style. It is designed as an open space with adjacent verandas and uses natural, unpainted wood and white plaster. This helps to emphasize the surrounding landscape. The walls and fenestration also affect the views from inside the pavilion. Most of the walls are made of shutters that can vary the amount of light and air into the pavilion and change the view by controlling the shutters' heights. The second floor, called ''The Tower of Sound Waves'' (潮音洞, Chō-on-dō ), is built in the style of warrior aristocrats, or ''[[:en:Shinden-zukuri|Shinden-zukuri]]''. On this floor, sliding wood doors and latticed windows create a feeling of impermanence. The second floor also contains a Buddha Hall and a shrine dedicated to the goddess of mercy, Kannon. The third floor is built in traditional [[:en:Chinese Chán|Chinese ''chán'']] (Jpn. [[zen]]) style, also known as ''zenshū-[[:en:Main Hall (Japanese Buddhism)|Main Hall (Japanese Buddhism)]]-zukuri''. It is called the ''Cupola of the Ultimate'' (究竟頂, Kukkyō-chō). The zen typology depicts a more religious ambiance in the pavilion, as was popular during the Muromachi period. The roof is in a thatched pyramid with shingles.Young, David, Michiko Young, and Tan Hong. The material culture of Death in medieval Japan. North Claredon, VT: Turtle Publishing, 2005. N. pag. Print. The building is topped with a bronze [[:en:Fenghuang|''hōō'']] (phoenix) ornament. From the outside, viewers can see gold plating added to the upper stories of the pavilion. The gold leaf covering the upper stories hints at what is housed inside: the shrines. The outside is a reflection of the inside. The elements of nature, death, religion, are formed together to create this connection between the pavilion and outside intrusions. ===Garden design=== The Golden Pavilion is set in a Japanese {{nihongo|strolling garden|回遊式庭園|kaiyū-shiki-teien|lit. a landscape garden in the go-round style}}. The location implements the idea of [[:en:Borrowing of scenery ("shakkei")|Borrowing of scenery ("shakkei")]] that integrates the outside and the inside, creating an extension of the views surrounding the pavilion and connecting it with the outside world. The pavilion extends over a pond, called {{nihongo|''Kyōko-chi''|鏡湖池|Mirror Pond}}, that reflects the building. The pond contains 10 smaller islands. The zen typology is seen through the rock composition; the bridges and plants are arranged in a specific way to represent famous places in Chinese and Japanese literature. Vantage points and focal points were established because of the strategic placement of the pavilion to view the gardens surrounding the pavilion. A small {{nihongo|fishing hall|釣殿|tsuri-dono}} or roofed deck is attached to the rear of the pavilion building, allowing a small boat to be moored under it. The pavilion grounds were built according to descriptions of the [[Pure Land Buddhism#Early history|Western Paradise of the Buddha Amida]], intending to illustrate a harmony between heaven and earth. The largest [[:en:Islet|Islet]] in the pond represents the Japanese islands. The four stones forming a straight line in the pond near the pavilion are intended to represent sailboats anchored at night, bound for the ''Isle of Eternal Life'' in Chinese mythology. The garden complex is an excellent example of [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] garden design.''Eyewitness Travel Guides: Japan''. Dorling Kindersley Publishing (2000). {{ISBN|0-7894-5545-5}}. The Muromachi period is considered to be a classical age of Japanese garden design.“Pregil, Philip, and Nancy Volkman. Landscapes in History: Design and Planning in the Eastern and Western tradition. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons Inc., 1992. N. pag. Print.”. The correlation between buildings and its settings were greatly emphasized during this period. It was an artistic way to integrate the structure within the landscape. The garden designs were characterized by a reduction in scale, a more central purpose, and a distinct setting.Boults, Elizabeth, and Chip Sullivan. Illustrated History of Landscape Design. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons INc., 2010. N. pag. Print. A minimalistic approach was brought to the garden design by recreating larger landscapes in a smaller scale around a structure. ==Gallery== File:1930s Japan Travel Poster - 15.jpg|1930s travel poster File:Kinkaku-ji entrance.jpg|Entrance and ticket booth File:Kinkaku-ji close up.jpg|Kinkaku-ji close up File:Kinkaku-ji 03.jpg|Interior File:Kinkaku-ji garden.jpg|Kinkaku-ji garden File:Golden Pavillion 2010 03 29 32.jpg|The lower pond File:Yōshū Chikanobu Kinkaku haiken.jpg|[[Toyohara Chikanobu]] File:Kyoto-Kinkaku-ji-White-Snake.jpg|White Snake Pagoda of Kinkaku-ji File:Kinkaku-ji temple in Kyoto.jpg|Kinkaku-Ji, Kyoto in May 2019 File:Kinkakuji Keychain from Japan, from personal collection, photographed by Yogabrata Chakraborty, on May 6, 2023.jpg|Kinkaku-ji keychain ==See also== {{Portal|Japan|Religion|Gardening|Architecture}} * [[The Temple of the Golden Pavilion]] by Yukio Mishima, a novel loosely based on the 1950 destruction of Kinkaku-ji * [[:en:Buntenkaku|Buntenkaku]] in Nagoya, modeled after the Golden Pavilion * [[Ginkaku-ji]] * [[Shōkoku-ji]] * [[:en:Chūson-ji|Chūson-ji]] with golden Konjiki-dō * [[:en:Golden Tea Room|Golden Tea Room]] * [[:en:List of Special Places of Scenic Beauty, Special Historic Sites and Special Natural Monuments|List of Special Places of Scenic Beauty, Special Historic Sites and Special Natural Monuments]] * [[:en:Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)|Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)]] ==Notes== {{reflist|30em}} == References == * Boults, Elizabeth, and Chip Sullivan. ''Illustrated History of Landscape Design''. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2010. * Gerhart, Karen M. ''The Material Culture of Death in Medieval Japan''. Honolulu: University of Hawaii Press, 2009. * Pregil, Philip, and Nancy Volkman. ''Landscapes in History: Design and Planning in the Eastern and Western Tradition''. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 1992. * Young, David, and Michiko Young. ''The Art of Japanese Architecture''. North Claredon, VT: Periplus, 2005. == Further reading == *{{cite book |last= Kawaguchi |first= Yoko |title= Japanese Zen Gardens |location= London |publisher= Francis Lincoln |date= 2014 |type= Hardback |isbn= 978-0-7112-3447-5}} *[[Schirokauer, Conrad]]; Lurie, David; Gay, Suzanne (2005). {{Short description|Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan}} {{About|a Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan|other topics translated as "Temple of the Golden Pavilion" or "Golden Pavilion Temple" in English|Temple of the Golden Pavilion (disambiguation)}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Rokuon-ji | native_name = {{lang|ja|鹿苑寺}} | image = Kinkaku-ji the Golden Temple in Kyoto overlooking the lake - high rez.JPG | image_size = 350 | alt = | caption = The ''shariden'' at Rokuon-ji,
commonly known as the Golden Pavilion (''Kinkakuji'') {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=220}} | map_type = Japan | map_size = | map_alt = | map_caption = | location = 1 Kinkakuji-chō, [[:en:Kita-ku, Kyoto|Kita-ku]], [[:en:Kyoto|Kyōto]], [[:en:Kyoto Prefecture|Kyoto Prefecture]]{{cite web |url=http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/arrange/attractions/facilities/gardens/83dn3a000000ee6g.html |title=Tourist Facilities of Japan - Kinkaku-ji Temple Garden |publisher=Japan National Tourism Organization |access-date=2010-07-15}} | coordinates = {{Coord|35.0395|N|135.7285|E|format=dms|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | religious_affiliation = [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] | sect =[[Zen]], [[Rinzai]] sect, [[Shōkoku-ji]] school | deity = [[:en:Avalokiteśvara|Kannon Bosatsu]] (Avalokiteśvara) | country = Japan | functional_status = | website = {{URL|https://www.shokoku-ji.jp/en/kinkakuji/|www.shokoku-ji.jp/en/kinkakuji/}} | founded_by = [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshimitsu|Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]] | year_completed = 1397
1955 (reconstruction) }} {{nihongo|'''Kinkaku-ji'''|金閣寺||{{literally}} 'Temple of the Golden Pavilion'}}, officially named {{nihongo|'''Rokuon-ji'''|鹿苑寺||{{literally|[[Sarnath|Deer Garden]] Temple}}}}, is a [[Zen]] [[:en:Buddhist temples in Japan|Buddhist temple]] in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{cite web |url=http://www.orientalarchitecture.com/japan/kyoto/kinkakuji.php |title=Kinkakuji Temple - 金阁寺, Kyoto, Japan |publisher=Oriental Architecture |access-date=2010-07-13}} It is one of the most popular buildings in Kyoto, attracting many visitors annually.Bornoff, Nicholas (2000). ''The National Geographic Traveler: Japan''. National Geographic Society. {{ISBN|0-7922-7563-2}}. It is designated as a National Special Historic Site, a National Special Landscape and is one of 17 locations making up the [[:en:Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)|Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto]] which are [[World Heritage Site]]s.{{cite web |url=http://kyoto.asanoxn.com/places/ps_popularity.htm |title=Places of Interest in Kyoto (Top 15 most visited places in Kyoto by visitors from overseas) |publisher=Asano Noboru |access-date=2010-07-15}} ==History== is peeling off due to deterioration over time.]] The site of Kinkaku-ji was originally a villa called ''Kitayama-dai'' (北山第), belonging to a powerful statesman, [[Saionji Kintsune]].{{cite web |url=http://kyoto.asanoxn.com/places/kinkaku/kinkakuji.htm |title=Kinkaku-ji in Kyoto |publisher=Asano Noboru |access-date=2010-07-15}} Kinkaku-ji's history dates to 1397, when the villa was purchased from the Saionji family by ''[[shōgun]]'' [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshimitsu|Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]] and transformed into the Kinkaku-ji complex. When Yoshimitsu died the building was converted into a [[Zen Buddhism|Zen]] temple by his son, according to his wishes.Scott, David (1996). ''Exploring Japan''. Fodor's Travel Publications, Inc. {{ISBN|0-679-03011-5}}.{{page number|date=June 2020}} During the [[:en:Ōnin war|Ōnin war]] (1467–1477), all of the buildings in the complex aside from the pavilion were burned down. On 2 July 1950, at 2:30 am, the pavilion was burned down{{cite web |last1=Cartwright |first1=Mark |title=Kinkakuji |url=https://www.worldhistory.org/Kinkakuji/ |website=World History Encyclopedia |publisher=UNESCO |access-date=23 March 2021}} by a 22-year-old novice monk, Hayashi Yoken ([[:en:Kinkaku-ji arson|Kinkaku-ji arson incident]]), who then attempted suicide on the Daimon-ji hill behind the building. He survived, and was subsequently taken into custody. The monk was sentenced to seven years in prison, but was released because of mental illnesses ([[:en:persecution complex|persecution complex]] and [[schizophrenia]]) on 29 September 1955; he died of [[tuberculosis]] in March 1956.{{cite book|author=Albert Borowitz|title=Terrorism for self-glorification: the Herostratos syndrome|url=https://archive.org/details/terrorismforself0000boro|url-access=registration|access-date=1 July 2011|year=2005|publisher=Kent State University Press|isbn=978-0-87338-818-4|pages=[https://archive.org/details/terrorismforself0000boro/page/49 49]–62}} See: [[:en:Herostratos syndrome|Herostratos syndrome]] During the fire, the original statue of Ashikaga Yoshimitsu was lost to the flames (now restored). A fictionalized version of these events is at the center of [[Yukio Mishima]]'s 1956 book ''[[The Temple of the Golden Pavilion]]'', and another in the ballet ''[[RAkU (ballet)| RAkU]]''. The present pavilion structure dates from 1955, when it was rebuilt. The pavilion is three stories high, {{convert|12.5|m|ft|adj=off|sp=us|abbr=off|-1}} in height.Young, David, and Michiko Young. The art of Japanese Architecture. North Claredon, VT: Turtle Publishing, 2007. N. pag. Print.{{page number|date=June 2020}} The reconstruction is said to be a close copy of the original, although some have questioned whether such an extensive gold-leaf coating was used on the original structure. {{Short description|Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan}} {{About|a Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan|other topics translated as "Temple of the Golden Pavilion" or "Golden Pavilion Temple" in English|Temple of the Golden Pavilion (disambiguation)}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Rokuon-ji | native_name = {{lang|ja|鹿苑寺}} | image = Kinkaku-ji the Golden Temple in Kyoto overlooking the lake - high rez.JPG | image_size = 350 | alt = | caption = The ''shariden'' at Rokuon-ji,
commonly known as the Golden Pavilion (''Kinkakuji'') {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=220}} | map_type = Japan | map_size = | map_alt = | map_caption = | location = 1 Kinkakuji-chō, [[:en:Kita-ku, Kyoto|Kita-ku]], [[:en:Kyoto|Kyōto]], [[:en:Kyoto Prefecture|Kyoto Prefecture]]{{cite web |url=http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/arrange/attractions/facilities/gardens/83dn3a000000ee6g.html |title=Tourist Facilities of Japan - Kinkaku-ji Temple Garden |publisher=Japan National Tourism Organization |access-date=2010-07-15}} | coordinates = {{Coord|35.0395|N|135.7285|E|format=dms|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | religious_affiliation = [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] | sect =[[Zen]], [[Rinzai]] sect, [[Shōkoku-ji]] school | deity = [[:en:Avalokiteśvara|Kannon Bosatsu]] (Avalokiteśvara) | country = Japan | functional_status = | website = {{URL|https://www.shokoku-ji.jp/en/kinkakuji/|www.shokoku-ji.jp/en/kinkakuji/}} | founded_by = [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshimitsu|Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]] | year_completed = 1397
1955 (reconstruction) }} {{nihongo|'''Kinkaku-ji'''|金閣寺||{{literally}} 'Temple of the Golden Pavilion'}}, officially named {{nihongo|'''Rokuon-ji'''|鹿苑寺||{{literally|[[Sarnath|Deer Garden]] Temple}}}}, is a [[Zen]] [[:en:Buddhist temples in Japan|Buddhist temple]] in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{cite web |url=http://www.orientalarchitecture.com/japan/kyoto/kinkakuji.php |title=Kinkakuji Temple - 金阁寺, Kyoto, Japan |publisher=Oriental Architecture |access-date=2010-07-13}} It is one of the most popular buildings in Kyoto, attracting many visitors annually.Bornoff, Nicholas (2000). ''The National Geographic Traveler: Japan''. National Geographic Society. {{ISBN|0-7922-7563-2}}. It is designated as a National Special Historic Site, a National Special Landscape and is one of 17 locations making up the [[:en:Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)|Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto]] which are [[World Heritage Site]]s.{{cite web |url=http://kyoto.asanoxn.com/places/ps_popularity.htm |title=Places of Interest in Kyoto (Top 15 most visited places in Kyoto by visitors from overseas) |publisher=Asano Noboru |access-date=2010-07-15}} ==History== is peeling off due to deterioration over time.]] The site of Kinkaku-ji was originally a villa called ''Kitayama-dai'' (北山第), belonging to a powerful statesman, [[Saionji Kintsune]].{{cite web |url=http://kyoto.asanoxn.com/places/kinkaku/kinkakuji.htm |title=Kinkaku-ji in Kyoto |publisher=Asano Noboru |access-date=2010-07-15}} Kinkaku-ji's history dates to 1397, when the villa was purchased from the Saionji family by ''[[shōgun]]'' [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshimitsu|Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]] and transformed into the Kinkaku-ji complex. When Yoshimitsu died the building was converted into a [[Zen Buddhism|Zen]] temple by his son, according to his wishes.Scott, David (1996). ''Exploring Japan''. Fodor's Travel Publications, Inc. {{ISBN|0-679-03011-5}}.{{page number|date=June 2020}} During the [[:en:Ōnin war|Ōnin war]] (1467–1477), all of the buildings in the complex aside from the pavilion were burned down. On 2 July 1950, at 2:30 am, the pavilion was burned down{{cite web |last1=Cartwright |first1=Mark |title=Kinkakuji |url=https://www.worldhistory.org/Kinkakuji/ |website=World History Encyclopedia |publisher=UNESCO |access-date=23 March 2021}} by a 22-year-old novice monk, Hayashi Yoken ([[:en:Kinkaku-ji arson|Kinkaku-ji arson incident]]), who then attempted suicide on the Daimon-ji hill behind the building. He survived, and was subsequently taken into custody. The monk was sentenced to seven years in prison, but was released because of mental illnesses ([[:en:persecution complex|persecution complex]] and [[schizophrenia]]) on 29 September 1955; he died of [[tuberculosis]] in March 1956.{{cite book|author=Albert Borowitz|title=Terrorism for self-glorification: the Herostratos syndrome|url=https://archive.org/details/terrorismforself0000boro|url-access=registration|access-date=1 July 2011|year=2005|publisher=Kent State University Press|isbn=978-0-87338-818-4|pages=[https://archive.org/details/terrorismforself0000boro/page/49 49]–62}} See: [[:en:Herostratos syndrome|Herostratos syndrome]] During the fire, the original statue of Ashikaga Yoshimitsu was lost to the flames (now restored). A fictionalized version of these events is at the center of [[Yukio Mishima]]'s 1956 book ''[[The Temple of the Golden Pavilion]]'', and another in the ballet ''[[:en:RAkU (ballet)| RAkU]]''. The present pavilion structure dates from 1955, when it was rebuilt. The pavilion is three stories high, {{convert|12.5|m|ft|adj=off|sp=us|abbr=off|-1}} in height.Young, David, and Michiko Young. The art of Japanese Architecture. North Claredon, VT: Turtle Publishing, 2007. N. pag. Print.{{page number|date=June 2020}} The reconstruction is said to be a close copy of the original, although some have questioned whether such an extensive gold-leaf coating was used on the original structure. In 1984, it was discovered that the gold leaf on the reconstructed building had peeled off, and from 1986 to 1987, it was replaced with 0.5 μm gold leaf, five times the thickness of the gold leaf on the reconstructed building. Although Japanese gold leaf has become thinner with the passage of time due to improved technology, the 0.5 μm gold leaf is as thick as traditional Japanese gold leaf.{{cite web|url=http://www.koetsuan.jp/kinkaku/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211023011422/http://www.koetsuan.jp/kinkaku/index.html|script-title=ja:金閣寺大修復 金閣修復 五倍箔|language=ja|author=Kazuo Yaguchi|archive-date=23 October 2021|access-date=30 October 2022}} Additionally, the interior of the building, including the paintings and Yoshimitsu's statue, were also restored. Finally, the roof was restored in 2003. The name Kinkaku (金閣 ''gold pavilion'') is derived from the gold leaf that the pavilion is covered in. Gold was an important addition to the pavilion because of its underlying meaning. The gold employed was intended to mitigate and purify any pollution or negative thoughts and feelings towards death.Gerhart, Karen M. The material culture of Death in medieval Japan. N.p.: University of Hawaii Press, 2009. N. pag. Print.{{page number|date=June 2020}} Other than the symbolic meaning behind the gold leaf, the Muromachi period heavily relied on visual excesses. With the focus on the Golden Pavilion, the way that the structure is mainly covered in that material creates an impression that stands out because of the sunlight reflecting and the effect the reflection creates on the pond. {{clear|left}} ==Design details== [[File:Kinkaku-ji 04.jpg|thumb|right|Roof ornament]] The {{nihongo|Golden Pavilion|金閣|Kinkaku}} is a three-story building on the grounds of the Rokuon-ji temple complex. The top two stories of the pavilion are covered with pure [[:en:Gold leaf|Gold leaf]]. The pavilion functions as a ''shariden'' (舎利殿), housing relics of the [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Buddha]] (Buddha's Ashes). The building was an important model for [[Ginkaku-ji]] (Silver Pavilion Temple) and [[Shōkoku-ji]], which are also located in Kyoto. When these buildings were constructed, [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshimasa|Ashikaga Yoshimasa]] employed the styles used at Kinkaku-ji and even borrowed the names of its second and third floors. ===Architectural design=== [[File:Kinkakuji Kyoto05s3s3990.jpg|thumb|left|The fishing deck and small islets at the rear of the pavilion]] The pavilion successfully incorporates three distinct styles of architecture, which are shinden, samurai and zen, specifically on each floor. Each floor of the Kinkaku uses a different architectural style. The first floor, called ''The Chamber of Dharma Waters'' (法水院, Hō-sui-in), is rendered in ''[[shinden-zukuri]]'' style, reminiscent of the residential style of the 11th century [[:en:Heian period|Heian]] imperial aristocracy. It is evocative of the Shinden palace style. It is designed as an open space with adjacent verandas and uses natural, unpainted wood and white plaster. This helps to emphasize the surrounding landscape. The walls and fenestration also affect the views from inside the pavilion. Most of the walls are made of shutters that can vary the amount of light and air into the pavilion and change the view by controlling the shutters' heights. The second floor, called ''The Tower of Sound Waves'' (潮音洞, Chō-on-dō ), is built in the style of warrior aristocrats, or ''[[:en:Shinden-zukuri|Shinden-zukuri]]''. On this floor, sliding wood doors and latticed windows create a feeling of impermanence. The second floor also contains a Buddha Hall and a shrine dedicated to the goddess of mercy, Kannon. The third floor is built in traditional [[:en:Chinese Chán|Chinese ''chán'']] (Jpn. [[zen]]) style, also known as ''zenshū-[[:en:Main Hall (Japanese Buddhism)|Main Hall (Japanese Buddhism)]]-zukuri''. It is called the ''Cupola of the Ultimate'' (究竟頂, Kukkyō-chō). The zen typology depicts a more religious ambiance in the pavilion, as was popular during the Muromachi period. The roof is in a thatched pyramid with shingles.Young, David, Michiko Young, and Tan Hong. The material culture of Death in medieval Japan. North Claredon, VT: Turtle Publishing, 2005. N. pag. Print. The building is topped with a bronze [[:en:Fenghuang|''hōō'']] (phoenix) ornament. From the outside, viewers can see gold plating added to the upper stories of the pavilion. The gold leaf covering the upper stories hints at what is housed inside: the shrines. The outside is a reflection of the inside. The elements of nature, death, religion, are formed together to create this connection between the pavilion and outside intrusions. ===Garden design=== The Golden Pavilion is set in a Japanese {{nihongo|strolling garden|回遊式庭園|kaiyū-shiki-teien|lit. a landscape garden in the go-round style}}. The location implements the idea of [[:en:Borrowing of scenery ("shakkei")|Borrowing of scenery ("shakkei")]] that integrates the outside and the inside, creating an extension of the views surrounding the pavilion and connecting it with the outside world. The pavilion extends over a pond, called {{nihongo|''Kyōko-chi''|鏡湖池|Mirror Pond}}, that reflects the building. The pond contains 10 smaller islands. The zen typology is seen through the rock composition; the bridges and plants are arranged in a specific way to represent famous places in Chinese and Japanese literature. Vantage points and focal points were established because of the strategic placement of the pavilion to view the gardens surrounding the pavilion. A small {{nihongo|fishing hall|釣殿|tsuri-dono}} or roofed deck is attached to the rear of the pavilion building, allowing a small boat to be moored under it. The pavilion grounds were built according to descriptions of the [[Pure Land Buddhism#Early history|Western Paradise of the Buddha Amida]], intending to illustrate a harmony between heaven and earth. The largest [[:en:Islet|Islet]] in the pond represents the Japanese islands. The four stones forming a straight line in the pond near the pavilion are intended to represent sailboats anchored at night, bound for the ''Isle of Eternal Life'' in Chinese mythology. The garden complex is an excellent example of [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] garden design.''Eyewitness Travel Guides: Japan''. Dorling Kindersley Publishing (2000). {{ISBN|0-7894-5545-5}}. The Muromachi period is considered to be a classical age of Japanese garden design.“Pregil, Philip, and Nancy Volkman. Landscapes in History: Design and Planning in the Eastern and Western tradition. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons Inc., 1992. N. pag. Print.”. The correlation between buildings and its settings were greatly emphasized during this period. It was an artistic way to integrate the structure within the landscape. The garden designs were characterized by a reduction in scale, a more central purpose, and a distinct setting.Boults, Elizabeth, and Chip Sullivan. Illustrated History of Landscape Design. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons INc., 2010. N. pag. Print. A minimalistic approach was brought to the garden design by recreating larger landscapes in a smaller scale around a structure. ==Gallery== File:1930s Japan Travel Poster - 15.jpg|1930s travel poster File:Kinkaku-ji entrance.jpg|Entrance and ticket booth File:Kinkaku-ji close up.jpg|Kinkaku-ji close up File:Kinkaku-ji 03.jpg|Interior File:Kinkaku-ji garden.jpg|Kinkaku-ji garden File:Golden Pavillion 2010 03 29 32.jpg|The lower pond File:Yōshū Chikanobu Kinkaku haiken.jpg|[[Toyohara Chikanobu]] File:Kyoto-Kinkaku-ji-White-Snake.jpg|White Snake Pagoda of Kinkaku-ji File:Kinkaku-ji temple in Kyoto.jpg|Kinkaku-Ji, Kyoto in May 2019 File:Kinkakuji Keychain from Japan, from personal collection, photographed by Yogabrata Chakraborty, on May 6, 2023.jpg|Kinkaku-ji keychain ==See also== {{Portal|Japan|Religion|Gardening|Architecture}} * [[The Temple of the Golden Pavilion]] by Yukio Mishima, a novel loosely based on the 1950 destruction of Kinkaku-ji * [[:en:Buntenkaku|Buntenkaku]] in Nagoya, modeled after the Golden Pavilion * [[Ginkaku-ji]] * [[Shōkoku-ji]] * [[:en:Chūson-ji|Chūson-ji]] with golden Konjiki-dō * [[:en:Golden Tea Room|Golden Tea Room]] * [[:en:List of Special Places of Scenic Beauty, Special Historic Sites and Special Natural Monuments|List of Special Places of Scenic Beauty, Special Historic Sites and Special Natural Monuments]] * [[:en:Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)|Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)]] ==Notes== {{reflist|30em}} == References == * Boults, Elizabeth, and Chip Sullivan. ''Illustrated History of Landscape Design''. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2010. * Gerhart, Karen M. ''The Material Culture of Death in Medieval Japan''. Honolulu: University of Hawaii Press, 2009. * Pregil, Philip, and Nancy Volkman. ''Landscapes in History: Design and Planning in the Eastern and Western Tradition''. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 1992. * Young, David, and Michiko Young. ''The Art of Japanese Architecture''. North Claredon, VT: Tuttle Publishing, 2007. * Young, David, Michiko Young, and Tan Hong. ''Introduction to Japanese Architecture''. North Claredon, VT: Periplus, 2005. == Further reading == *{{cite book |last= Kawaguchi |first= Yoko |title= Japanese Zen Gardens |location= London |publisher= Francis Lincoln |date= 2014 |type= Hardback |isbn= 978-0-7112-3447-5}} *[[Schirokauer, Conrad]]; Lurie, David; Gay, Suzanne (2005). A Brief History of Japanese Civilization. Wadsworth Publishing. {{ISBN|978-0-618-91522-4}}. OCLC 144227752. ==External links== {{Commons Category:11]] [[Category|Kinkaku-ji}} * [https://www.shokoku-ji.jp/en/kinkakuji/ Official site of Kinkaku-ji] * [http://www.orientalarchitecture.com/japan/kyoto/kinkakuji.php Oriental Architecture – Kinkakuji Temple] * [https://www.omamori.com/en/4_kinkaku-ji Omamori Charms Amulets of Kinkaku-ji Temple] * {{Osmway|98115917}} {{World Heritage Kyoto}} {{Buddhist temples in Japan}} {{draft categories| [[Category:1397 establishments]] [[Category:14th-century Buddhist temples]] [[Category:20th-century Buddhist temples]] [[Category:Buddhist temples in Kyoto]] [[Category:Important Cultural Properties of Japan]] [[Category:Myoshin-ji temples]] [[Category:Rebuilt buildings and structures in Japan]] [[Category:Religious buildings and structures completed in 1955]] [[Category:Special Historic Sites]] [[Category:Special Places of Scenic Beauty]] [[Category:World Heritage Sites in Japan]] }} [[image:Japon-1886-41.jpg|thumb|left|Painted photograph of the Golden Pavilion in 1885. On 2 July 1950, at 2:30 am, the pavilion was burned down{{cite web |last1=Cartwright |first1=Mark |title=Kinkakuji |url=https://www.worldhistory.org/Kinkakuji/ |website=World History Encyclopedia |publisher=UNESCO |access-date=23 March 2021}} by a 22-year-old novice monk, Hayashi Yoken ([[:en:Kinkaku-ji arson|Kinkaku-ji arson incident]]), who then attempted suicide on the Daimon-ji hill behind the building. The monk was sentenced to seven years in prison, but was released because of mental illnesses ([[:en:persecution complex|persecution complex]] and [[schizophrenia]]) on 29 September 1955; he died of [[tuberculosis]] in March 1956.{{cite book|author=Albert Borowitz|title=Terrorism for self-glorification: the Herostratos syndrome|url=https://archive.org/details/terrorismforself0000boro|url-access=registration|access-date=1 July 2011|year=2005|publisher=Kent State University Press|isbn=978-0-87338-818-4|pages=[https://archive.org/details/terrorismforself0000boro/page/49 49]–62}} See: [[:en:Herostratos syndrome|Herostratos syndrome]] During the fire, the original statue of Ashikaga Yoshimitsu was lost to the flames (now restored). A fictionalized version of these events is at the center of [[Yukio Mishima]]'s 1956 book ''[[The Temple of the Golden Pavilion]]'', and another in the ballet ''[[:en:RAkU (ballet)| RAkU]]''. The present pavilion structure dates from 1955, when it was rebuilt. The pavilion is three stories high, {{convert|12.5|m|ft|adj=off|sp=us|abbr=off|-1}} in height.Young, David, and Michiko Young. The art of Japanese Architecture. North Claredon, VT: Turtle Publishing, 2007. N. pag. Print.{{page number|date=June 2020}} The reconstruction is said to be a close copy of the original, although some have questioned whether such an extensive gold-leaf coating was used on the original structure. In 1984, it was discovered that the gold leaf on the reconstructed building had peeled off, and from 1986 to 1987, it was replaced with 0.5 μm gold leaf, five times the thickness of the gold leaf on the reconstructed building. Although Japanese gold leaf has become thinner with the passage of time due to improved technology, the 0.5 μm gold leaf is as thick as traditional Japanese gold leaf.{{cite web|url=http://www.koetsuan.jp/kinkaku/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211023011422/http://www.koetsuan.jp/kinkaku/index.html|script-title=ja:金閣寺大修復 金閣修復 五倍箔|language=ja|author=Kazuo Yaguchi|archive-date=23 October 2021|access-date=30 October 2022}} Additionally, the interior of the building, including the paintings and Yoshimitsu's statue, were also restored. Finally, the roof was restored in 2003. The name Kinkaku (金閣 ''gold pavilion'') is derived from the gold leaf that the pavilion is covered in. Gold was an important addition to the pavilion because of its underlying meaning. The gold employed was intended to mitigate and purify any pollution or negative thoughts and feelings towards death.Gerhart, Karen M. The material culture of Death in medieval Japan. N.p.: University of Hawaii Press, 2009. N. pag. Print.{{page number|date=June 2020}} Other than the symbolic meaning behind the gold leaf, the Muromachi period heavily relied on visual excesses. With the focus on the Golden Pavilion, the way that the structure is mainly covered in that material creates an impression that stands out because of the sunlight reflecting and the effect the reflection creates on the pond. {{clear|left}} ==Design details== [[File:Kinkaku-ji 04.jpg|thumb|right|Roof ornament]] The {{nihongo|Golden Pavilion|金閣|Kinkaku}} is a three-story building on the grounds of the Rokuon-ji temple complex. The top two stories of the pavilion are covered with pure [[:en:Gold leaf|Gold leaf]]. The pavilion functions as a ''shariden'' (舎利殿), housing relics of the [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Buddha]] (Buddha's Ashes). The building was an important model for [[Ginkaku-ji]] (Silver Pavilion Temple) and [[Shōkoku-ji]], which are also located in Kyoto. When these buildings were constructed, [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshimasa|Ashikaga Yoshimasa]] employed the styles used at Kinkaku-ji and even borrowed the names of its second and third floors. ===Architectural design=== [[File:Kinkakuji Kyoto05s3s3990.jpg|thumb|left|The fishing deck and small islets at the rear of the pavilion]] The pavilion successfully incorporates three distinct styles of architecture, which are shinden, samurai and zen, specifically on each floor. Each floor of the Kinkaku uses a different architectural style. The first floor, called ''The Chamber of Dharma Waters'' (法水院, Hō-sui-in), is rendered in ''[[shinden-zukuri]]'' style, reminiscent of the residential style of the 11th century [[:en:Heian period|Heian]] imperial aristocracy. It is evocative of the Shinden palace style. It is designed as an open space with adjacent verandas and uses natural, unpainted wood and white plaster. This helps to emphasize the surrounding landscape. The walls and fenestration also affect the views from inside the pavilion. Most of the walls are made of shutters that can vary the amount of light and air into the pavilion and change the view by controlling the shutters' heights. The second floor, called ''The Tower of Sound Waves'' (潮音洞, Chō-on-dō ), is built in the style of warrior aristocrats, or ''[[:en:Shinden-zukuri|Shinden-zukuri]]''. On this floor, sliding wood doors and latticed windows create a feeling of impermanence. The second floor also contains a Buddha Hall and a shrine dedicated to the goddess of mercy, Kannon. The third floor is built in traditional [[:en:Chinese Chán|Chinese ''chán'']] (Jpn. [[zen]]) style, also known as ''zenshū-[[:en:Main Hall (Japanese Buddhism)|Main Hall (Japanese Buddhism)]]-zukuri''. It is called the ''Cupola of the Ultimate'' (究竟頂, Kukkyō-chō). The zen typology depicts a more religious ambiance in the pavilion, as was popular during the Muromachi period. The roof is in a thatched pyramid with shingles.Young, David, Michiko Young, and Tan Hong. The material culture of Death in medieval Japan. North Claredon, VT: Turtle Publishing, 2005. N. pag. Print. The building is topped with a bronze [[:en:Fenghuang|''hōō'']] (phoenix) ornament. From the outside, viewers can see gold plating added to the upper stories of the pavilion. The gold leaf covering the upper stories hints at what is housed inside: the shrines. The outside is a reflection of the inside. The elements of nature, death, religion, are formed together to create this connection between the pavilion and outside intrusions. ===Garden design=== The Golden Pavilion is set in a Japanese {{nihongo|strolling garden|回遊式庭園|kaiyū-shiki-teien|lit. a landscape garden in the go-round style}}. The location implements the idea of [[:en:Borrowing of scenery ("shakkei")|Borrowing of scenery ("shakkei")]] that integrates the outside and the inside, creating an extension of the views surrounding the pavilion and connecting it with the outside world. The pavilion extends over a pond, called {{nihongo|''Kyōko-chi''|鏡湖池|Mirror Pond}}, that reflects the building. The pond contains 10 smaller islands. The zen typology is seen through the rock composition; the bridges and plants are arranged in a specific way to represent famous places in Chinese and Japanese literature. Vantage points and focal points were established because of the strategic placement of the pavilion to view the gardens surrounding the pavilion. A small {{nihongo|fishing hall|釣殿|tsuri-dono}} or roofed deck is attached to the rear of the pavilion building, allowing a small boat to be moored under it. The pavilion grounds were built according to descriptions of the [[Pure Land Buddhism#Early history|Western Paradise of the Buddha Amida]], intending to illustrate a harmony between heaven and earth. The largest [[:en:Islet|Islet]] in the pond represents the Japanese islands. The four stones forming a straight line in the pond near the pavilion are intended to represent sailboats anchored at night, bound for the ''Isle of Eternal Life'' in Chinese mythology. The garden complex is an excellent example of [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] garden design.''Eyewitness Travel Guides: Japan''. Dorling Kindersley Publishing (2000). {{ISBN|0-7894-5545-5}}. The Muromachi period is considered to be a classical age of Japanese garden design.“Pregil, Philip, and Nancy Volkman. Landscapes in History: Design and Planning in the Eastern and Western tradition. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons Inc., 1992. N. pag. Print.”. The correlation between buildings and its settings were greatly emphasized during this period. It was an artistic way to integrate the structure within the landscape. The garden designs were characterized by a reduction in scale, a more central purpose, and a distinct setting.Boults, Elizabeth, and Chip Sullivan. Illustrated History of Landscape Design. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons INc., 2010. N. pag. Print. A minimalistic approach was brought to the garden design by recreating larger landscapes in a smaller scale around a structure. ==Gallery== File:1930s Japan Travel Poster - 15.jpg|1930s travel poster File:Kinkaku-ji entrance.jpg|Entrance and ticket booth File:Kinkaku-ji close up.jpg|Kinkaku-ji close up File:Kinkaku-ji 03.jpg|Interior File:Kinkaku-ji garden.jpg|Kinkaku-ji garden File:Golden Pavillion 2010 03 29 32.jpg|The lower pond File:Yōshū Chikanobu Kinkaku haiken.jpg|[[Toyohara Chikanobu]] File:Kyoto-Kinkaku-ji-White-Snake.jpg|White Snake Pagoda of Kinkaku-ji File:Kinkaku-ji temple in Kyoto.jpg|Kinkaku-Ji, Kyoto in May 2019 File:Kinkakuji Keychain from Japan, from personal collection, photographed by Yogabrata Chakraborty, on May 6, 2023.jpg|Kinkaku-ji keychain ==See also== {{Portal|Japan|Religion|Gardening|Architecture}} * [[The Temple of the Golden Pavilion]] by Yukio Mishima, a novel loosely based on the 1950 destruction of Kinkaku-ji * [[:en:Buntenkaku|Buntenkaku]] in Nagoya, modeled after the Golden Pavilion * [[Ginkaku-ji]] * [[Shōkoku-ji]] * [[:en:Chūson-ji|Chūson-ji]] with golden Konjiki-dō * [[:en:Golden Tea Room|Golden Tea Room]] * [[:en:List of Special Places of Scenic Beauty, Special Historic Sites and Special Natural Monuments|List of Special Places of Scenic Beauty, Special Historic Sites and Special Natural Monuments]] * [[:en:Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)|Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)]] ==Notes== {{reflist|30em}} == References == * Boults, Elizabeth, and Chip Sullivan. ''Illustrated History of Landscape Design''. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2010. * Gerhart, Karen M. ''The Material Culture of Death in Medieval Japan''. Honolulu: University of Hawaii Press, 2009. * Pregil, Philip, and Nancy Volkman. ''Landscapes in History: Design and Planning in the Eastern and Western Tradition''. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 1992. * Young, David, and Michiko Young. ''The Art of Japanese Architecture''. North Claredon, VT: Tuttle Publishing, 2007. * Young, David, Michiko Young, and Tan Hong. ''Introduction to Japanese Architecture''. North Claredon, VT: Periplus, 2005. == Further reading == *{{cite book |last= Kawaguchi |first= Yoko |title= Japanese Zen Gardens |location= London |publisher= Francis Lincoln |date= 2014 |type= Hardback |isbn= 978-0-7112-3447-5}} *[[Schirokauer, Conrad]]; Lurie, David; Gay, Suzanne (2005). A Brief History of Japanese Civilization. Wadsworth Publishing. {{ISBN|978-0-618-91522-4}}. 1955 (reconstruction) }} {{nihongo|'''Kinkaku-ji'''|金閣寺||{{literally}} 'Temple of the Golden Pavilion'}}, officially named {{nihongo|'''Rokuon-ji'''|鹿苑寺||{{literally|[[Sarnath|Deer Garden]] Temple}}}}, is a [[:en:Zen|Zen]] [[:en:Buddhist temples in Japan|Buddhist temple]] in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{cite web |url=http://www.orientalarchitecture.com/japan/kyoto/kinkakuji.php |title=Kinkakuji Temple - 金阁寺, Kyoto, Japan |publisher=Oriental Architecture |access-date=2010-07-13}} It is one of the most popular buildings in Kyoto, attracting many visitors annually.Bornoff, Nicholas (2000). When Yoshimitsu died the building was converted into a [[Zen Buddhism|Zen]] temple by his son, according to his wishes.Scott, David (1996). ''Exploring Japan''. Fodor's Travel Publications, Inc. {{ISBN|0-679-03011-5}}.{{page number|date=June 2020}} During the [[:en:Ōnin war|Ōnin war]] (1467–1477), all of the buildings in the complex aside from the pavilion were burned down. {{Short description|Zen Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan}} {{About|a Buddhist temple in Kyoto, Japan|other topics translated as "Temple of the Golden Pavilion" or "Golden Pavilion Temple" in English|Temple of the Golden Pavilion (disambiguation)}} {{Infobox religious building | name = Rokuon-ji | native_name = {{lang|ja|鹿苑寺}} | image = Kinkaku-ji the Golden Temple in Kyoto overlooking the lake - high rez.JPG | image_size = 350 | alt = | caption = The ''shariden'' at Rokuon-ji,
commonly known as the Golden Pavilion (''Kinkakuji'') {{Infobox mapframe|tyep=shape|zoom=14|frame-width=220}} | map_type = Japan | map_size = | map_alt = | map_caption = | location = 1 Kinkakuji-chō, [[:en:Kita-ku, Kyoto|Kita-ku]], [[:en:Kyoto|Kyōto]], [[:en:Kyoto Prefecture|Kyoto Prefecture]]{{cite web |url=http://www.jnto.go.jp/eng/arrange/attractions/facilities/gardens/83dn3a000000ee6g.html |title=Tourist Facilities of Japan - Kinkaku-ji Temple Garden |publisher=Japan National Tourism Organization |access-date=2010-07-15}} | coordinates = {{Coord|35.0395|N|135.7285|E|format=dms|region:JP_type:landmark|display=title,inline}} | religious_affiliation = [[:en:Buddhism|Buddhism]] | sect =[[:en:Zen|Zen]], [[Rinzai]] sect, [[Shōkoku-ji]] school | deity = [[:en:Avalokiteśvara|Kannon Bosatsu]] (Avalokiteśvara) | country = Japan | functional_status = | website = {{URL|https://www.shokoku-ji.jp/en/kinkakuji/|www.shokoku-ji.jp/en/kinkakuji/}} | founded_by = [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshimitsu|Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]] | year_completed = 1397
1955 (reconstruction) }} {{nihongo|'''Kinkaku-ji'''|金閣寺||{{literally}} 'Temple of the Golden Pavilion'}}, officially named {{nihongo|'''Rokuon-ji'''|鹿苑寺||{{literally|[[Sarnath|Deer Garden]] Temple}}}}, is a [[:en:Zen|Zen]] [[:en:Buddhist temples in Japan|Buddhist temple]] in [[:en:Kyoto|Kyoto]], [[:en:Japan|Japan]].{{cite web |url=http://www.orientalarchitecture.com/japan/kyoto/kinkakuji.php |title=Kinkakuji Temple - 金阁寺, Kyoto, Japan |publisher=Oriental Architecture |access-date=2010-07-13}} It is one of the most popular buildings in Kyoto, attracting many visitors annually.Bornoff, Nicholas (2000). ''The National Geographic Traveler: Japan''. National Geographic Society. {{ISBN|0-7922-7563-2}}. It is designated as a National Special Historic Site, a National Special Landscape and is one of 17 locations making up the [[:en:Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)|Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto]] which are [[World Heritage Site]]s.{{cite web |url=http://kyoto.asanoxn.com/places/ps_popularity.htm |title=Places of Interest in Kyoto (Top 15 most visited places in Kyoto by visitors from overseas) |publisher=Asano Noboru |access-date=2010-07-15}} ==History== is peeling off due to deterioration over time.]] The site of Kinkaku-ji was originally a villa called ''Kitayama-dai'' (北山第), belonging to a powerful statesman, [[:en:Saionji Kintsune|Saionji Kintsune]].{{cite web |url=http://kyoto.asanoxn.com/places/kinkaku/kinkakuji.htm |title=Kinkaku-ji in Kyoto |publisher=Asano Noboru |access-date=2010-07-15}} Kinkaku-ji's history dates to 1397, when the villa was purchased from the Saionji family by ''[[shōgun]]'' [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshimitsu|Ashikaga Yoshimitsu]] and transformed into the Kinkaku-ji complex. When Yoshimitsu died the building was converted into a [[:en:Zen|Zen]] temple by his son, according to his wishes.Scott, David (1996). ''Exploring Japan''. Fodor's Travel Publications, Inc. {{ISBN|0-679-03011-5}}.{{page number|date=June 2020}} During the [[:en:Ōnin war|Ōnin war]] (1467–1477), all of the buildings in the complex aside from the pavilion were burned down. On 2 July 1950, at 2:30 am, the pavilion was burned down{{cite web |last1=Cartwright |first1=Mark |title=Kinkakuji |url=https://www.worldhistory.org/Kinkakuji/ |website=World History Encyclopedia |publisher=UNESCO |access-date=23 March 2021}} by a 22-year-old novice monk, Hayashi Yoken ([[:en:Kinkaku-ji arson|Kinkaku-ji arson incident]]), who then attempted suicide on the Daimon-ji hill behind the building. He survived, and was subsequently taken into custody. The monk was sentenced to seven years in prison, but was released because of mental illnesses ([[:en:persecution complex|persecution complex]] and [[schizophrenia]]) on 29 September 1955; he died of [[tuberculosis]] in March 1956.{{cite book|author=Albert Borowitz|title=Terrorism for self-glorification: the Herostratos syndrome|url=https://archive.org/details/terrorismforself0000boro|url-access=registration|access-date=1 July 2011|year=2005|publisher=Kent State University Press|isbn=978-0-87338-818-4|pages=[https://archive.org/details/terrorismforself0000boro/page/49 49]–62}} See: [[:en:Herostratos syndrome|Herostratos syndrome]] During the fire, the original statue of Ashikaga Yoshimitsu was lost to the flames (now restored). A fictionalized version of these events is at the center of [[Yukio Mishima]]'s 1956 book ''[[The Temple of the Golden Pavilion]]'', and another in the ballet ''[[:en:RAkU (ballet)| RAkU]]''. The present pavilion structure dates from 1955, when it was rebuilt. The pavilion is three stories high, {{convert|12.5|m|ft|adj=off|sp=us|abbr=off|-1}} in height.Young, David, and Michiko Young. The art of Japanese Architecture. North Claredon, VT: Turtle Publishing, 2007. N. pag. Print.{{page number|date=June 2020}} The reconstruction is said to be a close copy of the original, although some have questioned whether such an extensive gold-leaf coating was used on the original structure. In 1984, it was discovered that the gold leaf on the reconstructed building had peeled off, and from 1986 to 1987, it was replaced with 0.5 μm gold leaf, five times the thickness of the gold leaf on the reconstructed building. Although Japanese gold leaf has become thinner with the passage of time due to improved technology, the 0.5 μm gold leaf is as thick as traditional Japanese gold leaf.{{cite web|url=http://www.koetsuan.jp/kinkaku/index.html|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20211023011422/http://www.koetsuan.jp/kinkaku/index.html|script-title=ja:金閣寺大修復 金閣修復 五倍箔|language=ja|author=Kazuo Yaguchi|archive-date=23 October 2021|access-date=30 October 2022}} Additionally, the interior of the building, including the paintings and Yoshimitsu's statue, were also restored. Finally, the roof was restored in 2003. The name Kinkaku (金閣 ''gold pavilion'') is derived from the gold leaf that the pavilion is covered in. Gold was an important addition to the pavilion because of its underlying meaning. The gold employed was intended to mitigate and purify any pollution or negative thoughts and feelings towards death.Gerhart, Karen M. The material culture of Death in medieval Japan. N.p.: University of Hawaii Press, 2009. N. pag. Print.{{page number|date=June 2020}} Other than the symbolic meaning behind the gold leaf, the Muromachi period heavily relied on visual excesses. With the focus on the Golden Pavilion, the way that the structure is mainly covered in that material creates an impression that stands out because of the sunlight reflecting and the effect the reflection creates on the pond. {{clear|left}} ==Design details== [[File:Kinkaku-ji 04.jpg|thumb|right|Roof ornament]] The {{nihongo|Golden Pavilion|金閣|Kinkaku}} is a three-story building on the grounds of the Rokuon-ji temple complex. The top two stories of the pavilion are covered with pure [[:en:Gold leaf|Gold leaf]]. The pavilion functions as a ''shariden'' (舎利殿), housing relics of the [[:en:Gautama Buddha|Buddha]] (Buddha's Ashes). The building was an important model for [[Ginkaku-ji]] (Silver Pavilion Temple) and [[Shōkoku-ji]], which are also located in Kyoto. When these buildings were constructed, [[:en:Ashikaga Yoshimasa|Ashikaga Yoshimasa]] employed the styles used at Kinkaku-ji and even borrowed the names of its second and third floors. ===Architectural design=== [[File:Kinkakuji Kyoto05s3s3990.jpg|thumb|left|The fishing deck and small islets at the rear of the pavilion]] The pavilion successfully incorporates three distinct styles of architecture, which are shinden, samurai and zen, specifically on each floor. Each floor of the Kinkaku uses a different architectural style. The first floor, called ''The Chamber of Dharma Waters'' (法水院, Hō-sui-in), is rendered in ''[[shinden-zukuri]]'' style, reminiscent of the residential style of the 11th century [[:en:Heian period|Heian]] imperial aristocracy. It is evocative of the Shinden palace style. It is designed as an open space with adjacent verandas and uses natural, unpainted wood and white plaster. This helps to emphasize the surrounding landscape. The walls and fenestration also affect the views from inside the pavilion. Most of the walls are made of shutters that can vary the amount of light and air into the pavilion and change the view by controlling the shutters' heights. The second floor, called ''The Tower of Sound Waves'' (潮音洞, Chō-on-dō ), is built in the style of warrior aristocrats, or ''[[:en:Shinden-zukuri|Shinden-zukuri]]''. On this floor, sliding wood doors and latticed windows create a feeling of impermanence. The second floor also contains a Buddha Hall and a shrine dedicated to the goddess of mercy, Kannon. The third floor is built in traditional [[:en:Chinese Chán|Chinese ''chán'']] (Jpn. [[:en:Zen|Zen]]) style, also known as ''zenshū-[[:en:Main Hall (Japanese Buddhism)|Main Hall (Japanese Buddhism)]]-zukuri''. It is called the ''Cupola of the Ultimate'' (究竟頂, Kukkyō-chō). The zen typology depicts a more religious ambiance in the pavilion, as was popular during the Muromachi period. The roof is in a thatched pyramid with shingles.Young, David, Michiko Young, and Tan Hong. The material culture of Death in medieval Japan. North Claredon, VT: Turtle Publishing, 2005. N. pag. Print. The building is topped with a bronze [[:en:Fenghuang|''hōō'']] (phoenix) ornament. From the outside, viewers can see gold plating added to the upper stories of the pavilion. The gold leaf covering the upper stories hints at what is housed inside: the shrines. The outside is a reflection of the inside. The elements of nature, death, religion, are formed together to create this connection between the pavilion and outside intrusions. ===Garden design=== The Golden Pavilion is set in a Japanese {{nihongo|strolling garden|回遊式庭園|kaiyū-shiki-teien|lit. a landscape garden in the go-round style}}. The location implements the idea of [[:en:Borrowing of scenery ("shakkei")|Borrowing of scenery ("shakkei")]] that integrates the outside and the inside, creating an extension of the views surrounding the pavilion and connecting it with the outside world. The pavilion extends over a pond, called {{nihongo|''Kyōko-chi''|鏡湖池|Mirror Pond}}, that reflects the building. The pond contains 10 smaller islands. The zen typology is seen through the rock composition; the bridges and plants are arranged in a specific way to represent famous places in Chinese and Japanese literature. Vantage points and focal points were established because of the strategic placement of the pavilion to view the gardens surrounding the pavilion. A small {{nihongo|fishing hall|釣殿|tsuri-dono}} or roofed deck is attached to the rear of the pavilion building, allowing a small boat to be moored under it. The pavilion grounds were built according to descriptions of the [[Pure Land Buddhism#Early history|Western Paradise of the Buddha Amida]], intending to illustrate a harmony between heaven and earth. The largest [[:en:Islet|Islet]] in the pond represents the Japanese islands. The four stones forming a straight line in the pond near the pavilion are intended to represent sailboats anchored at night, bound for the ''Isle of Eternal Life'' in Chinese mythology. The garden complex is an excellent example of [[:en:Muromachi period|Muromachi period]] garden design.''Eyewitness Travel Guides: Japan''. Dorling Kindersley Publishing (2000). {{ISBN|0-7894-5545-5}}. The Muromachi period is considered to be a classical age of Japanese garden design.“Pregil, Philip, and Nancy Volkman. Landscapes in History: Design and Planning in the Eastern and Western tradition. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons Inc., 1992. N. pag. Print.”. The correlation between buildings and its settings were greatly emphasized during this period. It was an artistic way to integrate the structure within the landscape. The garden designs were characterized by a reduction in scale, a more central purpose, and a distinct setting.Boults, Elizabeth, and Chip Sullivan. Illustrated History of Landscape Design. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons INc., 2010. N. pag. Print. A minimalistic approach was brought to the garden design by recreating larger landscapes in a smaller scale around a structure. ==Gallery== File:1930s Japan Travel Poster - 15.jpg|1930s travel poster File:Kinkaku-ji entrance.jpg|Entrance and ticket booth File:Kinkaku-ji close up.jpg|Kinkaku-ji close up File:Kinkaku-ji 03.jpg|Interior File:Kinkaku-ji garden.jpg|Kinkaku-ji garden File:Golden Pavillion 2010 03 29 32.jpg|The lower pond File:Yōshū Chikanobu Kinkaku haiken.jpg|[[Toyohara Chikanobu]] File:Kyoto-Kinkaku-ji-White-Snake.jpg|White Snake Pagoda of Kinkaku-ji File:Kinkaku-ji temple in Kyoto.jpg|Kinkaku-Ji, Kyoto in May 2019 File:Kinkakuji Keychain from Japan, from personal collection, photographed by Yogabrata Chakraborty, on May 6, 2023.jpg|Kinkaku-ji keychain ==See also== {{Portal|Japan|Religion|Gardening|Architecture}} * [[The Temple of the Golden Pavilion]] by Yukio Mishima, a novel loosely based on the 1950 destruction of Kinkaku-ji * [[:en:Buntenkaku|Buntenkaku]] in Nagoya, modeled after the Golden Pavilion * [[Ginkaku-ji]] * [[Shōkoku-ji]] * [[:en:Chūson-ji|Chūson-ji]] with golden Konjiki-dō * [[:en:Golden Tea Room|Golden Tea Room]] * [[:en:List of Special Places of Scenic Beauty, Special Historic Sites and Special Natural Monuments|List of Special Places of Scenic Beauty, Special Historic Sites and Special Natural Monuments]] * [[:en:Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)|Historic Monuments of Ancient Kyoto (Kyoto, Uji and Otsu Cities)]] ==Notes== {{reflist|30em}} == References == * Boults, Elizabeth, and Chip Sullivan. ''Illustrated History of Landscape Design''. Hoboken, NJ: John Wiley & Sons, 2010. * Gerhart, Karen M. ''The Material Culture of Death in Medieval Japan''.
